name: Cipactli
description: Cipactli opens the sequence of twenty day signs with the image of a powerful crocodilian earth creature. Its toothed jaws and rough hide belong to a being at home in water and on land, where the edge of a marsh becomes solid ground. In Nahua creation traditions, a great aquatic creature provides the body from which the earth takes shape. The sign gathers that image of emergence into the count of days, giving beginnings a living, physical form. Its earth is fertile and sustaining, yet also immense and consuming. The ridges of a crocodilian's back can recall the raised soil of a planted field, joining the animal's formidable body with the ground that holds seeds and supports human life.
meaning_and_glyph: Cipactli names a crocodilian or fantastic aquatic earth being. Its glyph often shows a long snout and conspicuous teeth, with features that may combine more than one animal. The image belongs to a sacred pictorial vocabulary rather than a precise modern species portrait. Some forms emphasize the jaws or head, while others suggest a creature emerging from water. It occupies the first position in the twenty-sign sequence, before Ehecatl, Wind.
symbolism: Beginnings and the formation of earth are central to Cipactli's symbolism. Water and land meet in the body of the creature, bringing the conditions of growth into a single image. The earth can feed living beings and receive them again, so its generative power includes an unsettling capacity to consume. Cipactli gives this relationship teeth, skin, and weight. Its position at the opening of the sequence reinforces the theme of origin, while the crocodilian form keeps that origin rooted in an animate world of water, soil, and living bodies.
cultural_context: Nahua creation narratives describe the ordered world taking shape through the transformation of a primordial earth being. Cipactli participates in this imagery alongside accounts of Tlaltecuhtli, the living earth. These narratives place human settlement and cultivation upon a foundation with its own sacred force. The image also recalls the ordinary environments where people encountered crocodilians, including rivers and marshes. As a calendrical sign, this creature enters a recurring sequence of days, allowing the memory of watery origins and the formation of land to recur within the human reckoning of time.

name: Ehecatl
description: Ehecatl is Wind, the moving air felt against the skin and seen in bending plants, drifting clouds, and scattered seeds. Its glyph often takes the form of a face wearing a projecting wind mask associated with Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl. The sign brings an invisible force into view through its effects on the living world. A light breeze can cool a field, while a storm drives rain across the earth with force. Wind also suggests breath and the air through which voices and music travel. The image of a sower suits its movement among dry plants, carrying seeds toward new ground. Within the count of days, Ehecatl gives shape to this restless exchange between the open sky, cultivated earth, and the breath of living beings.
meaning_and_glyph: Ehecatl means wind or air. The day glyph commonly uses a head with an elongated, beaklike mask, a familiar feature of Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl imagery. The projection makes blowing air visible through the form of a face. Although it can resemble a bird's beak, it identifies the wind-associated figure within this pictorial setting. Ehecatl is the second sign, following Cipactli and preceding Calli, House, in the recurring sequence of twenty.
symbolism: Wind connects movement with the conditions that sustain life. It carries clouds over planted ground and scatters the seeds of dry grasses. Breath gives the same element an intimate presence within the body. Voice, singing, and the sounds of rustling vegetation extend its symbolism into expression and listening. Gentle air and destructive gusts belong to this same force, giving the sign both delicacy and power. Ehecatl's imagery joins these effects through something that remains unseen in itself but continually alters the things it touches and the spaces through which it moves.
cultural_context: Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl is a wind-associated divine form in central Mexican religion. The projecting mask makes this figure recognizable in sculpture and painted imagery. Wind's place in accounts of cosmic motion also gives it a role beyond local weather. At the scale of fields and households, the arrival of wind could announce rain or scatter the seeds of another season. Its sacred associations therefore grew beside familiar experiences of breathing and cultivation. The calendar carries that relationship into named time, giving an otherwise invisible natural force a distinct place among animals, plants, and objects.

name: Calli
description: Calli means House, an enclosure that gathers life within walls and a roof. Its image evokes shelter from weather, a place for work, and the household where food and knowledge pass between generations. The sign's sense of containment also reaches beyond a dwelling to the wider idea of something held and protected. A vessel shelters its contents just as a building shelters the activities inside. Calli therefore draws attention to the interior, the space where daily life takes shape away from the open ground. In Nahua communities, houses belonged to family relationships and household ritual as well as production. Calli also names years within the calendrical cycle, giving the familiar outline of a building a place in the reckoning of longer spans of time.
meaning_and_glyph: Calli means house or building. Its glyph depicts an architectural enclosure, often recognizable through its roof and entrance. The doorway gives the image an inside and an outside, making the act of sheltering visible. The word's associations include a built space that contains or protects, while the sign itself remains a house. Calli is third in the twenty-sign order and is also one of the four signs used to name years.
symbolism: Containment is the organizing image of Calli. A house makes protected room for the people and activities within it, giving shelter a material shape. The symbolism reaches into provision, household continuity, and the care of things that must be kept. An interior can also suggest inward attention, the private space where experience and memory reside. These meanings grow out of the relation between an enclosure and its contents. Calli makes that relation tangible through a building, where protection depends upon an everyday structure maintained and used by a household.
cultural_context: The Nahua household was a place of production and ritual as well as residence. Work, family relationships, and inheritance helped connect each house with the wider community. Calli's calendrical role extends this domestic image across a much longer span. Together with Tochtli, Acatl, and Tecpatl, it belongs to the four signs used in year names. Their combinations with the thirteen numerals form a cycle of fifty-two years. A house could therefore appear both as the sign of a day and as part of a year name, within distinct but related counts.

name: Cuetzpalin
description: Cuetzpalin is Lizard, the small reptile that keeps close to the earth and breaks its stillness with a sudden run. Its long body and tail give the day sign an immediate sense of movement across stones and low vegetation. The animal belongs to the ground people cultivate and walk upon, bringing a familiar living presence into sacred time. In central Mexican imagery, the lizard also appears in connections with fertility and sexuality, where the vitality of animal life becomes a way to picture the earth's capacity to generate. Quiet observation and quick motion sit together in this image. Cuetzpalin draws its force from the creature's physical presence, a body pressed against the soil, alert and ready to move.
meaning_and_glyph: Cuetzpalin means lizard; Cuetzpalli is another form used for the name. Its glyph shows a small reptile with an elongated body and tail, sometimes with its limbs spread beside it. The animal's outline makes the sign recognizable without requiring one precise species identification. Its low posture distinguishes it from the larger crocodilian imagery of Cipactli. Cuetzpalin occupies the fourth position in the twenty-day sequence, between Calli, House, and Coatl, Serpent.
symbolism: The lizard brings bodily vitality into the sign's imagery. Its close contact with the ground connects it with the earth, while its rapid movement supplies an image of active life. Fertility and sexuality enter through this attention to living bodies and their capacity to continue life. In painted religious imagery, the lizard can appear within explicitly sexual settings. Its significance therefore includes the earth's generative qualities alongside the immediate impression of a quick, agile animal. The sign's power remains concrete, held in the posture and movement of a small creature.
cultural_context: Animals observed around fields and settlements supplied much of the day-sign vocabulary. The lizard offered a familiar example of a creature that could remain still and then move with startling speed. In central Mexican religious imagery, its associations extend into sexuality and fertility. Related calendrical discussions also bring dance and pleasure into this sphere through Huehuecoyotl, the Old Coyote. The animal sign and the dancing divine figure occupy different roles, but their connection places bodily life within a ceremonial setting as well as the ordinary environment of stones, soil, and plants.

name: Coatl
description: Coatl means Serpent, whose winding body gives motion a continuous, flowing outline. Snakes move across the earth with their whole bodies, and their shed skins offer a visible image of change. Serpent imagery fills Mesoamerican sacred art, appearing with feathers, jewels, or rattles and reaching into watery and celestial settings. In the figure of Coatlicue, interwoven serpents become a skirt, joining the animal with the earth's generative force. Other images bring two serpents together or combine the serpent with precious feathers. Coatl gathers this rich vocabulary into a day sign whose meanings depend upon the form and setting of the image. Its curves evoke living movement and the powerful connections between earth, water, and the sacred beings that inhabit them.
meaning_and_glyph: Coatl means serpent or snake. The glyph may show the head alone or include a curved body, sometimes with visible fangs or a forked tongue. More elaborate serpent images can carry feathers, jewels, or rattles, each changing the surrounding meaning. The day sign identifies the serpent within this wider family of sacred forms. Coatl is fifth in the twenty-sign order, following the lizard and preceding Miquiztli, Death, in the calendar's recurring count.
symbolism: The serpent's undulating body supplies a compelling image of living motion. Its contact with the earth and its appearances in aquatic imagery connect it with fertility and water. Skin shedding adds a natural image of altered form. Paired or double-headed serpents can bring complementary forces into one body, while feathered forms join the reptile with the air and precious adornment. These meanings arise through particular combinations of image and setting. The sign belongs to a sacred vocabulary in which the serpent can move between earthly and celestial realms without losing its recognizable animal form.
cultural_context: Serpents appear in sculpture, painted manuscripts, and accounts of creation across Mesoamerica. Quetzalcoatl joins serpent and precious-feather imagery, while Coatlicue's serpent skirt gives a different form to the relationship between living creatures and the earth. In Nahua creation narratives, great serpents also participate in shaping the world. These settings show how widely serpent forms could operate within sacred thought. Coatl places the animal within the sequence of named days, beside other beings drawn from the natural world, while retaining the broad religious associations that made its image so powerful.

name: Miquiztli
description: Miquiztli means Death and takes the direct form of a skull. The image brings mortality into the count of days as part of the same world that holds growth and flowering. Its symbolism reaches toward passage, the quiet interval after activity, and the changes through which living matter returns to the earth. A field can lie still before another season, and dry vegetation can become part of the ground that supports new growth. These natural images give death a place within continuing relationships between bodies and earth. Miquiztli also opens onto the sacred geography of the dead, where different journeys and destinations formed part of Nahua religious life. The skull gives these themes a stark, recognizable presence within recurring time.
meaning_and_glyph: Miquiztli literally means death. Its glyph usually depicts a human skull, with the exposed teeth and empty eye socket making its subject unmistakable. Skeletal imagery identifies the sign through the remains of a body rather than through a living animal or tool. Miquiztli is the sixth sign in the twenty-day sequence. It follows Coatl, Serpent, and precedes Mazatl, Deer, placing death within a continuous order that includes many forms of life.
symbolism: Miquiztli brings an ending into relationship with what follows it. The image of death can accompany reflection on transformation and intervals of stillness. Resting ground and vegetation that dries before another season provide natural comparisons for this movement between cessation and renewed activity. The skull also preserves the reality of mortality within these associations. Its symbolism includes the body's end and the ways living communities understand their ties to the dead. Within the count, the sign returns repeatedly, making mortality a recurring presence among the forces and beings that name time.
cultural_context: Nahua accounts of death describe different postmortem destinations and journeys according to the circumstances of dying. Mortuary practices and offerings maintained relationships between the living and those who had died. Death imagery also belonged to ceremonial settings where sacrifice, decomposition, and fertility could be closely connected. These religious relationships gave skeletal forms a place throughout sacred visual culture. The Miquiztli sign draws upon that world, bringing the recognizable skull into the tonalpohualli alongside images of plants and living animals. Its context includes both the loss of bodily life and a continuing sacred order.

name: Mazatl
description: Mazatl is Deer, an animal of the hills and wooded country beyond cultivated ground. Its raised ears and slender body evoke a creature attentive to nearby sounds and quick to disappear through the brush. Wind and rain belong to the world it inhabits, where open slopes meet dense cover and the day brings changing warmth. Deer supplied food, hides, and bone, making the relationship between people and this animal both practical and ceremonial. Hunting placed human lives in direct contact with the movement and vulnerability of wild beings. As a day sign, Mazatl carries that encounter into the count of time. Its image holds the alert presence of an animal whose life belongs to the mountains as well as to the history of human subsistence.
meaning_and_glyph: Mazatl means deer, a name that can encompass more than one species. The glyph usually identifies the animal through its head, prominent ears, and, in many depictions, antlers. These features make it distinct among the animal signs even when the whole body is absent. Full-body images can emphasize the slender legs and agile posture. Mazatl occupies the seventh position, following Miquiztli, Death, and preceding Tochtli, Rabbit, within the sequence of twenty.
symbolism: The deer evokes attentive presence and movement through uncultivated ground. Its ears and posture make listening visible, while its speed suggests the difficulty of approaching a wild animal. Associations with the Sun and warmth add another aspect to this image of active life in the hills. Hunting gives the same animal a relationship with sustenance and offering. The sign thus brings together the living creature in its own surroundings and the human dependence upon it. Its symbolism remains tied to an encounter with a consequential animal, its body, and the places where it lives.
cultural_context: Deer had economic and ritual importance across Mesoamerica. Meat, hides, and bone connected them with subsistence and the making of useful objects, while hunting and offerings placed them within ceremonial relationships. Their presence in imagery extended beyond their immediate use as resources. Mazatl brought the animal into the sacred count, where its familiar form could recur as a named day. Mountain environments and the spaces beyond settlement give this sign much of its distinctive setting. The deer belongs to a world people entered to hunt and gather, alongside the cultivated world that sustained their households.

name: Tochtli
description: Tochtli means Rabbit, a small, swift animal with a large place in the imagination of the Moon. Its familiar outline appears within lunar imagery, where a rabbit rests inside a curved vessel surrounded by water signs. The animal also evokes fertility and the abundance of living things. In central Mexican religion, rabbit imagery belongs to the world of maguey and pulque, the fermented drink used in social and ceremonial life. Pleasure and the possibility of excess share this setting, giving the sign a richer texture than simple abundance. Tochtli is also one of the four signs used to name years. The rabbit therefore moves through several kinds of recurring time, appearing in the daily count, in lunar images, and in the longer pattern of year names.
meaning_and_glyph: Tochtli means rabbit. Its day glyph often uses a head with long upright ears, making the animal easy to distinguish from the dog and feline signs. In lunar images the rabbit may appear with its body inside a curved, vessel-like outline. This surrounding frame belongs to the Moon's imagery, while the rabbit remains the named animal. Tochtli is eighth in the day-sign sequence and also belongs to the four signs used in year names.
symbolism: Rabbit symbolism brings fertility into contact with enjoyment and abundance. Its lunar setting gives those themes a recurring visual form, with the animal visible in the face of the Moon or held inside a water-marked vessel. Maguey and pulque extend this symbolism into the pleasures of drinking and ceremonial gathering. Abundance can invite celebration and also raise the question of proper measure. These relationships give Tochtli a place among images of pleasure and its limits, grounded in an animal known for quick movement and the frequent appearance of young.
cultural_context: The Centzon Totochtin, or Four Hundred Rabbits, are divine beings associated with the many forms or effects of pulque intoxication. Pulque, made from maguey sap, had social and ceremonial roles in central Mexico. Rabbit imagery connects this religious complex with the broader themes of fertility and enjoyment. Tochtli also has a separate calendrical role as a year-bearing sign, alongside Calli, Acatl, and Tecpatl. Their combinations with thirteen numerals create fifty-two year names. The same animal can therefore take part in lunar storytelling, ritual imagery, and the formal naming of years.

name: Atl
description: Atl is Water, the liquid that fills a jar, follows an irrigation channel, and spreads across a lake. Its changing form makes the sign an image of adaptation, while its steady flow suggests persistence and the capacity to reshape the ground. Water quenches thirst and nourishes fields, tying household life to rivers and springs. A still pool can hold the reflection of the sky; a swollen river can carry a force no vessel can contain. Both belong to Atl's meaning. In the lake environment of central Mexico, water also made travel and urban life possible. The sign gathers these familiar experiences into a sacred substance, precious because crops, bodies, and communities all depend upon its presence and its movement.
meaning_and_glyph: Atl means water. Its glyph commonly uses curling or flowing bands, often blue, with shell-like or jewel-like details. These forms give direction and visible edges to a substance that continually changes shape. Painted water can appear as a stream, a patterned band, or an element contained within another image. Atl is the ninth sign of the twenty, distinct from Quiahuitl, which specifically names rain falling from the sky onto the earth.
symbolism: Water suggests receptiveness through the way it takes the shape of its container. Its movement supplies a different image, of sustained force that wears away stone or becomes a dangerous flood. These qualities sit beside its immediate necessity for life and cultivation. Clear water can evoke cleansing, and a still expanse can become a mirror. Lakes and rivers also appear as precious ornaments of the earth. The sign holds these associations together through the material itself, whether carried in a household vessel or moving through a channel toward planted ground.
cultural_context: The Basin of Mexico's lakes and springs shaped settlement, agriculture, and travel. Tenochtitlan occupied a managed lake environment where channels and water routes formed part of daily life. Sacred relationships with water included mountains and springs as well as rain, with figures such as Chalchiuhtlicue and Tlaloc belonging to this wider religious world. Water's value lay in ordinary needs and in the forces beyond human control that could sustain or threaten a community. Atl places that substance within the calendar, connecting named days with an element present throughout household and public life.

name: Itzcuintli
description: Itzcuintli means Dog, the familiar animal that accompanies people beyond the house and returns with them at the end of the day. Its image brings companionship and protection into the count of time, grounded in the close relationship between dogs and human households. That relationship also extends into Nahua accounts of death. A dog could accompany the dead toward Mictlan and help them cross the water encountered on the journey. The animal that knows the paths around a home becomes a helper on a route beyond the living world. Itzcuintli holds these two settings together, the ordinary journey through fields and hills and the difficult passage after death. Its sacred importance grows out of the same proximity that made dogs such familiar household beings.
meaning_and_glyph: Itzcuintli means dog. The day glyph typically depicts the animal's head, using the muzzle and ears to establish its identity. Painted examples may include dark markings around the eye or spotted coloring. The sign represents the dog within a broad history of human companionship and animal keeping. Itzcuintli occupies the tenth position in the twenty-day sequence, following Atl, Water, and preceding Ozomahtli, Monkey, at the midpoint of the ordered signs.
symbolism: Companionship gives the dog its strongest symbolic connection with human life. Guarding a house, walking beside people, and returning home provide concrete images of attachment and assistance. The journey toward Mictlan extends that relationship across the boundary of death. In this setting the dog becomes a guide and helper, especially where the dead must cross water. Its familiarity gives this sacred role an intimate character. The sign brings the household animal into a wider geography of passage, where help can come through a relationship already known in daily life.
cultural_context: Dogs lived in Mesoamerican households and had several practical and ceremonial roles. Some were raised for food, while dog images also appear in objects associated with burial and the dead. Central Mexican mortuary traditions describe a dog accompanying a person toward Mictlan and assisting with the crossing of water. These associations give the animal a place in both domestic life and the sacred understanding of death. Itzcuintli gathers that connection into the named-day sequence, where a familiar creature carries the memory of human dependence upon companionship during difficult journeys.

name: Ozomahtli
description: Ozomahtli is Monkey, whose climbing body and quick gestures give the sign an air of play and lively movement. The spider monkey's agility among branches offers a natural image for the grace of dance, while its expressive face recalls the amusement of performance. In central Mexican imagery, the monkey is closely connected with music and artistic activity. Song and movement give shared feeling a visible and audible form, much as the animal's actions catch the attention of those watching it. Ozomahtli brings this world of performance into the calendar through a creature associated with warm forests and the movement of branches overhead. Its joy is bodily and social, shaped by rhythm, gesture, and the pleasure of watching a living being move.
meaning_and_glyph: Ozomahtli means monkey. The glyph generally shows a monkey's head, with the face and surrounding hair giving it a distinctive outline. The spider monkey is a common identification in discussions of the sign's animal imagery. Full-body representations can emphasize climbing limbs and an expressive pose. Ozomahtli is eleventh in the sequence of twenty signs, following Itzcuintli, Dog, and preceding Malinalli, Grass, within the continually repeating count of named days.
symbolism: The monkey connects agile movement with amusement and artistic expression. A climbing animal's changing gestures offer a visual parallel to dance, while its lively social presence belongs naturally beside performance and music. These associations place delight in the body and in the experience shared between a performer and an audience. Ozomahtli also belongs near the religious sphere of Xochipilli, where pleasure and artistic activity have sacred significance. The sign gives this sphere an animal form, full of motion and recognizable expression, rather than representing the arts through a musical instrument alone.
cultural_context: Monkeys connected the warm lowlands with the cities of the central Mexican highlands through the movement of animals and goods. Merchant caravans brought them to places such as Tenochtitlan and Tetzcuco, where people could encounter them within households. Their gestures and agility made them striking subjects for imagery. The broader association of monkeys with music and dance places them within the ceremonial world of performance as well as everyday amusement. Ozomahtli therefore brings a creature of forest branches into an urban and religious setting, where the arts held an important place in collective life.

name: Malinalli
description: Malinalli is Grass, especially the long leaves that can be gathered, twisted, and woven into useful material. Its image begins with an ordinary plant that covers hills in the rainy season, dries as conditions change, and returns with another period of growth. This alternation gives the sign a strong connection with renewal through the earth. The plant's usefulness adds a different kind of transformation, as separate blades become a binding or a woven object in human hands. Some glyphs show grass emerging from a fleshless jaw, bringing new vegetation and the remains of a body into one image. Malinalli draws its meaning from these concrete changes, where what dries or falls apart can enter another cycle and where simple leaves become something that holds together.
meaning_and_glyph: Malinalli is commonly translated as grass or twisted grass. Glyphs may show a tuft or bundle with long leaves and a flowering spike. Other forms place the growing plant above a fleshless jaw, or use the jaw itself to identify the day. This variation gives the sign a distinctive combination of vegetal and skeletal imagery. Malinalli is twelfth in the twenty-sign sequence, immediately before Acatl, Reed, another plant used in everyday material life.
symbolism: Renewal is visible in the grass's seasonal changes. Green growth gives way to dryness and becomes part of the earth before another cycle brings the hills to life. Skeletal elements in the glyph place the remains of life beside its return. Twisting and weaving introduce human work into this pattern, turning loose leaves into cords and bindings. Malinalli's symbolism therefore joins recurring growth with the ability to make a useful form from gathered material. Both meanings depend on transformation that can be seen and handled, in vegetation and in the things made from it.
cultural_context: Grasses supplied materials for bindings, woven objects, and other practical uses in Mesoamerican communities. Long leaves could be twisted together or interlaced, drawing upon techniques shared with other useful plants. The plant's seasonal presence also made it a familiar measure of changing conditions on the hills. Malinalli's calendrical image places this ordinary material within a sacred setting, sometimes beside the jaw of a dead being. Its relationship with Miquiztli, Death, rests on the theme of renewal through intervals of decline, while the grass retains its own identity as growing and workable material.

name: Acatl
description: Acatl means Reed, the straight stem rising from damp ground and the edges of water channels. Its hollow form can become a flute, while other stems supply shafts for arrows and tools. The sign joins the plant's rooted growth with the directions human hands give its material. Painted forms may show a clump beside water or a bound group of shafts tipped like darts. Reeds also appear within imagery of ceremonial fire, linking the plant with an action that brings heat into the human world. Acatl has a larger role in naming time as one of the four year-bearing signs. Its image therefore reaches beyond the water's edge into craft, ceremony, and the remembered dates through which communities ordered their histories.
meaning_and_glyph: Acatl means reed. Its glyph can show growing stems emerging beside a water channel, or a bound group of reeds that resembles a bundle of darts. Adornments such as down or tassels appear in some ceremonial forms. The image may emphasize the plant itself or the straight shafts people make from it. Acatl is thirteenth in the day-sign sequence and is also one of the four signs used in year names.
symbolism: The reed's straight growth gives the sign a clear sense of direction. When stems become shafts, that shape takes on purpose through their use as tools or projectiles. A hollow stem can also carry breath as a flute, turning the plant into sound. Associations with ceremonial fire bring heat into the same material world of skill and action. These meanings keep Acatl connected to a plant that grows in wet places while extending it into human making. The living reed and the prepared shaft remain recognizable parts of the same image.
cultural_context: Reeds belonged to the lake environments of central Mexico and supplied material for construction and many smaller objects. Acatl also appears in calendrical names associated with sacred and historical figures, including Ce Acatl Topiltzin Quetzalcoatl. Reed year names formed part of the cycle shared with House, Rabbit, and Flint, each combined with numerals one through thirteen. Their recurrence provided a way to name years and remember events. The sign's historical weight thus grew beside its practical familiarity, joining the readily available wetland plant with ceremonial implements and the recording of time.

name: Ocelotl
description: Ocelotl is Jaguar, the powerful spotted feline of Mesoamerican sacred imagery. Its rosettes, watchful posture, and quiet approach give the sign a force that belongs to both the living animal and the dark places associated with it. The spotted coat can evoke a sky filled with stars, while caves and mountain hollows bring the image into the earth's interior. Jaguar forms also appear in royal and martial settings, where the predator's strength becomes a visible expression of authority. These meanings gather around a creature whose presence can be concealed until the moment it moves. As a day sign, Ocelotl carries the density of night, the depth of mountains, and the physical power of a hunter into the recurring count.
meaning_and_glyph: Ocelotl is conventionally rendered Jaguar in the day-sign sequence. Its glyph typically uses a spotted feline head, with a strong jaw and dark markings. Full-body images may emphasize the rosettes and the animal's crouching or advancing posture. The sign's identity belongs to a long history of sacred feline imagery. It occupies the fourteenth position, following Acatl, Reed, and preceding Cuauhtli, Eagle, another animal prominent in imagery of power and warfare.
symbolism: Night and the earth's interior give jaguar imagery two closely related settings. Dark spots can suggest stars against the surrounding sky, while the animal's association with caves brings that darkness beneath the ground. Predatory strength adds the force of a body that approaches quietly and attacks with sudden power. The feline also appears as Tepeyolohtli, Heart of the Mountains, within sacred imagery of mountain depths. These associations give Ocelotl a meaning shaped by hidden presence and concentrated strength, grounded in the animal's form and extended through the spaces it evokes.
cultural_context: Jaguar imagery appears throughout Mesoamerica in sacred, royal, and martial contexts. In central Mexico, feline attire formed part of the military identity commonly called the jaguar warrior, often discussed beside eagle warriors. Images of Tepeyolohtli connect the animal with mountains and caves, while accounts of earlier cosmic eras include the Sun of Jaguar. These settings place the feline across several kinds of sacred and political meaning. Ocelotl carries that history into the tonalpohualli, where its image joins a calendrical order that also includes the eagle, serpent, and primordial earth creature.

name: Cuauhtli
description: Cuauhtli means Eagle, the high-flying predator whose sharp beak and commanding posture make it a powerful image of the sky. Its flight and hunting vision link the sign with height and the Sun's force, while its plumage belongs to ceremonial and military expressions of authority. An eagle can be distant above a mountain and suddenly close as it descends toward prey, bringing open space and concentrated action into one body. The animal also holds a central place in the Mexica account of Tenochtitlan's foundation, where it appears upon a cactus. As a day sign, Cuauhtli gathers these solar and political associations around a living bird, giving the wide sky a recognizable presence within the ordered count of time.
meaning_and_glyph: Cuauhtli means eagle. The glyph usually identifies the bird through its head and strong hooked beak, sometimes with plumage that accentuates the face. The beak distinguishes it from other bird signs, particularly the vulture. Full-body eagle images can emphasize broad wings or a poised, upright stance. Cuauhtli occupies the fifteenth position in the twenty-sign sequence, after Ocelotl, Jaguar, placing two animals prominent in military and sacred imagery beside one another.
symbolism: Height and solar force shape the eagle's symbolism. Its flight provides a visible link between the ground and the open sky, while keen vision and predatory movement give that link physical intensity. Eagle imagery also conveys authority through its place in martial attire and public emblems. The bird's relationship with the Sun makes its power celestial as well as terrestrial. These associations meet in the image of a body capable of rising above the inhabited world and returning with sudden force, a striking way to picture movement and strength within sacred art.
cultural_context: Eagle warriors and jaguar warriors occupied prominent places in Mexica military imagery. Their animal forms gave ceremonial dress a powerful visual language linked with warfare and sacred force. The eagle also appears in the foundation narrative of Tenochtitlan, perched upon a cactus in the place chosen for the city. This image later became part of Mexico's national emblem. The calendrical sign belongs to a wider and older Mesoamerican vocabulary, while these political uses show how strongly the bird could express a community's account of its origins and its public identity.

name: Cozcacuauhtli
description: Cozcacuauhtli is Vulture, a bird whose circling flight connects the open sky with the remains of life on the ground. Its bare head and feathered collar make a distinctive image among the day signs. Feeding on animals that have died gives the vulture a place where death becomes nourishment for another living body. The sign can therefore invite attention to the use of what remains and the continuation of life amid decay. Its imagery has also been connected with age and accumulated experience, bringing an elder's long view beside the bird's patient presence above the earth. Cozcacuauhtli holds these themes in a creature that descends toward what others leave behind, giving it a place within the ongoing life of the world.
meaning_and_glyph: Cozcacuauhtli is conventionally translated Vulture. The name is also rendered as collared eagle, and glyphs often emphasize a bare head, a hooked beak, or a conspicuous collar of feathers. These features distinguish the bird from the eagle sign. Particular depictions have been compared with king vultures, although the image need not identify one exact modern species. Cozcacuauhtli is sixteenth in the twenty-sign sequence, following Cuauhtli and preceding Ollin, Movement.
symbolism: The vulture's feeding places it at the meeting of mortality and continuing life. What remains after an animal dies becomes nourishment, giving the sign a concrete basis for reflection on use and renewal. Its circling flight brings this activity into a larger view of the fields and hills. Associations with age and experience add the idea of knowledge gathered over time. These meanings can sit beside one another without changing the bird into a simple emblem of death. Its presence depends upon what has ended, yet it remains an active living creature.
cultural_context: Vultures were familiar figures over the countryside, where their feeding made them visible around dead animals. Their distinctive heads and flight supplied a recognizable form for calendrical art. The sign's associations with age and counsel belong to a wider tradition of giving birds and animals social as well as sacred significance. The bird also appears within a varied regional calendrical world in which images and names could differ. Cozcacuauhtli's place in the sequence preserves a scavenger beside an eagle, allowing two very different relations between birds, sky, and the earth to appear in neighboring signs.

name: Ollin
description: Ollin means Movement, the activity visible in running water, a shifting body, or the daily course of the Sun. Its interlaced glyph gives this restless condition a compact form, with parts that seem to turn around a center. The sign's meaning reaches beyond any single motion to a world continually changing through time. A beating heart offers an intimate image of that activity, while the Sun gives it a cosmic scale. Nahui Ollin, Four Movement, names the present cosmic era in Nahua tradition and has a central place in the imagery of the Sun Stone. Ollin brings this vast setting into the count of days through an image of motion, where life continues through activity and the world remains open to change.
meaning_and_glyph: Ollin means movement. Its glyph commonly has interlaced or opposed parts arranged around a center, producing a distinctive abstract form among the animal and plant signs. Four-pointed and lobed versions give motion an ordered visual pattern. Earthquake can be one expression of movement, while the name itself has a broader meaning. Ollin occupies the seventeenth place in the sequence, after Cozcacuauhtli, Vulture, and before Tecpatl, Flint, in the count of twenty.
symbolism: Movement connects living activity with the larger processes of the world. The heart's rhythm offers one bodily image, and flowing water gives another outside the body. Solar motion extends the same theme across the sky. Butterfly imagery can also express continual movement through the changing position of wings. These associations give Ollin a scale that includes immediate experience and the cosmos. Its abstract glyph gathers them into an organized pattern, making motion recognizable without depicting one animal or event. Change becomes the sign's subject, held in a form that itself suggests turning and relation.
cultural_context: Nahui Ollin, Four Movement, names the present cosmic era within Nahua accounts of successive worlds. The Sun Stone gives this sign a central role in a monumental arrangement that also refers to earlier eras. That setting makes movement part of the condition of the cosmos and its possible upheaval. Elsewhere, the sign belongs to the ordinary recurrence of the tonalpohualli, where it combines with different numerals. Its presence in both calendrical images and a major monument shows how one compact sign could participate in daily reckoning and an account of world history.

name: Tecpatl
description: Tecpatl means Flint, especially the sharp stone blade whose shaped edge turns a hard material into a cutting tool. Its glyph can be spare and pointed, or take on a face that gives the implement a living presence. Stone knives belonged to practical work and to ceremonies with profound sacred weight. The edge also offers an image of inquiry, cutting beneath an outer layer to reveal what lies inside. Sparks supply a related image of sudden light and the beginning of an idea. Tecpatl gathers these associations around an object made through skill, where controlled force produces an effective form. It is also one of the four signs used to name years, carrying the blade's familiar outline into a longer reckoning of time.
meaning_and_glyph: Tecpatl means flint and commonly identifies a flint knife or blade. The glyph usually has a pointed, leaflike outline with a cutting edge. Personified forms may add eyes, teeth, or a mouth, turning the implement into an animate image. Flint and obsidian both supplied stone blades, though they are distinct materials. Tecpatl is eighteenth in the sequence of twenty and also belongs to the four signs that take part in naming years.
symbolism: A cutting edge gives Tecpatl its central symbolic action. The blade separates and opens, offering a concrete image for examining what lies beneath an outer form. The flash of a spark adds an association with light and the sudden arrival of an idea. Cold wind can also be imagined as a sharp edge against the skin. These comparisons grow out of physical sensations and uses of stone. In sacred imagery, a face on the knife gives the object agency, expressing the force of an implement whose effects could carry great ritual consequence.
cultural_context: Mesoamerican communities shaped stone into blades for practical tasks and ceremonial use. Sacrificial knives held particular religious importance, and images could depict them as animate beings with faces and teeth. The object therefore belonged to material skill and to a sacred world in which implements could possess force of their own. Tecpatl's place among the year-bearing signs gives it another role beside Calli, Tochtli, and Acatl. Combined with numerals, those signs name the fifty-two years of a cycle, extending an everyday recognizable form into the recording and remembrance of longer time.

name: Quiahuitl
description: Quiahuitl means Rain, the water that arrives through the sky and changes the condition of a field. It softens dry ground and allows planted seeds to send up new growth, filling the hills with green. The sign also holds rain's dangerous force, when heavy downpours or hail damage the same crops they might have sustained. Its imagery often recalls Tlaloc through a ringed eye and a distinctive face in profile. In stories of the Tlaloque, rain comes from vessels broken above the clouds, bringing storm and nourishment into one vivid scene. Quiahuitl gives the uncertainty of rainfall a place in the count of days, joining human dependence on harvests with powers that gather beyond the reach of the hand.
meaning_and_glyph: Quiahuitl means rain or downpour. Its glyph can depict falling water or a rain-associated face with a large ring around the eye. The facial form recalls Tlaloc, making rain visible through a recognizable divine image. In some descriptions, two profile rain faces brought together form a frontal face. Quiahuitl is nineteenth in the sequence, after Tecpatl, Flint, and before Xochitl, Flower, near the end of the twenty recurring signs.
symbolism: Rain gives the sign a strong association with germination and agricultural abundance. Its arrival can release the potential of a planted seed and restore water to the ground. Storms reveal another aspect of the same force, capable of damaging crops through excess water or hail. The symbolism includes dependence upon a gift whose timing and intensity remain uncertain. Mountains and clouds provide the wider setting for this encounter between sky and soil. Quiahuitl expresses the moment water crosses that distance, reaching the fields as gentle moisture or a forceful downpour.
cultural_context: Rainfall shaped agricultural work in central Mexico, where maize and other crops depended on the season's water. Tlaloc and the Tlaloque belong to the sacred relationships linking rain with mountains, caves, and springs. Accounts of the Tlaloque breaking vessels above the clouds give storms an image of stored water suddenly released. Ceremonial attention to rain grew from the same dependence that made drought and hail serious threats. Quiahuitl brings this agricultural and religious world into the tonalpohualli, where a named day can recall both the hope for growing fields and the danger of destructive weather.

name: Xochitl
description: Xochitl means Flower and closes the sequence of twenty day signs with color, fragrance, and the promise of fruit. A flower marks a plant's growth while giving pleasure through its form, making it a powerful image for beauty and accomplishment. In Nahua expression, flowers also belong to song and poetry, where carefully made words can carry the preciousness of a blossom. The paired phrase in xochitl in cuicatl, flower and song, brings this connection into focus. Offerings and artistic activity give flowers a place in shared ceremonial life as well as in gardens and fields. Xochitl gathers these meanings into the end of the sequence, where flowering can express the fulfillment of work and the growth that makes another beginning possible.
meaning_and_glyph: Xochitl means flower. Its glyph presents a stylized blossom, often with open petals and a central form that makes the plant recognizable at a glance. Different depictions may vary in detail without naming one exact species. The image emphasizes flowering itself, the visible emergence of color and form from a living plant. Xochitl is the twentieth and final sign, followed again by Cipactli when the repeating sequence begins another round.
symbolism: Flowers connect sensory beauty with the development of living things. Color and fragrance make a blossom precious in the present, while its place before fruit gives flowering a sense of fulfillment and further possibility. These associations extend into human expression through song, poetry, and skilled making. A finished task can be compared with a flower offered to others, giving accomplishment a shared form. Xochitl's symbolism therefore includes delight and the care through which something comes to fullness. Its final place in the sequence reinforces this image of flowering before another return begins.
cultural_context: Flowers appeared in offerings and ceremonial adornment throughout Nahua life. Their beauty and fragrance connected them with pleasure, preciousness, and artistic expression. The phrase in xochitl in cuicatl, flower and song, joins floral imagery with poetry and elevated expression. Figures such as Xochiquetzal and Xochipilli belong to the broader sacred world of flowers and the arts. These relationships give the calendrical sign a rich cultural setting, where the same blossom can grow in a field, adorn an offering, or become an image through which a song expresses feeling and thought.
